newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ROTTERDAM PORT DISPUTE WORSENS, BUT EFFECT LIMITED.
newsitem.headline: ROTTERDAM PORT DISPUTE WORSENS, BUT EFFECT LIMITED.

text.p: A dispute involving port workers in Rotterdam escalated on Thursday with 300 on strike, but the port itself and individual companies were largely unaffected.
The strikers work for a company called SHB which contracts out its labour pool to companies in the port on a semi-permanent basis.
The dispute centres around plans by SHB's management to make 275 of its 975 employees redundant and to put 375 workers on a three-day week.
The Rotterdam port authority said ships were moving in and out of the port as normal.
Oil traders in the Rotterdam area said loading and unloading of crude and oil products also appeared unaffected.
"I'm not aware of any impact. We are generally just using our own employees," said a trader at a Rotterdam-based refiner.
The container and distribution sector appeared the only industry to have suffered.
European Combined Terminals (ECT) said it had missed the 40-50 SHB workers it frequently employs, but had called on its own workers to compensate for the lost manpower.
ECT had encountered difficulties, however, when its own workers took "solidarity" strike action on Wednesday and Thursday morning.
"This afternoon, there has been no repeat of the solidarity action. The sea side is working as normal. On the land side, there are longer waits for truckers," an ECT spokesman said.
ECT is owned by P&O Nedlloyd Containers, Internatio-Mueller, Pakhoed and Dutch Railways.
A spokesman from metal warehousing group Steinweg said the dispute had had no impact on its operations.
"It's not having any impact, the company is not very dependent on SHB workers," he said. "There has never been a strike that has had any effect on Steinweg."
Rotterdam-based meals and feeds traders said there had been no interruption to ships offloading and no market impact.
No-one at SHB or the Rotterdam branch of the transport union was immediately available for comment.
